blocks.text: Token optimization broadens the prompt compression idea covered in the previous topic into the full picture, both input and output tokens count toward total cost and latency, and strategies exist for controlling each, from word choice to explicit output length limits.

This topic covers why both input and output tokens matter, constraining output length directly, stop sequences, word choice effects on tokenization efficiency, avoiding wasteful formatting, and how this broader view differs from the prompt compression covered in the previous topic.
1. Token Optimization as the Broader Picture

blocks.alt: Building on prompt caching, token optimization covers total token efficiency

blocks.text: Where prompt compression, covered in the previous topic, focused specifically on shrinking the input prompt itself, token optimization covers the complete picture, every token that gets processed or generated in a single request, and the strategies for keeping that total number efficient.
2. Input Tokens and Output Tokens Both Count

blocks.alt: Input tokens and output tokens both count toward total cost

blocks.text: This connects back to the earlier Tokens and Tokenization topic, most model APIs charge for both the tokens sent in and the tokens generated in response, an application optimizing only the input prompt while ignoring an unnecessarily long, verbose output is only solving half the actual cost problem.
3. Constraining Output Length Directly

blocks.alt: No output length limit produces unpredictably long responses, an explicit max token setting bounds response length

blocks.text: Most model APIs accept an explicit maximum output token setting, capping how long a response can possibly be, combined with a clear length instruction in the prompt itself, covered in the earlier Output Format topic, this provides a direct, reliable lever for controlling output token cost.

code.content:
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4",
    messages=messages,
    max_tokens=150,  # hard cap on the response length
)

blocks.text: 4. Stop Sequences, Ending Generation Early

blocks.alt: When a stop sequence is reached, generation ends immediately

blocks.text: A stop sequence is a specific string that, once generated, immediately ends the response, useful for a structured output where you know exactly what marks the natural end of the content you actually need, stopping generation right there rather than letting the model continue generating tokens you will discard anyway.

blocks.text: 5. Word Choice and Tokenization Efficiency

blocks.alt: A rare word choice uses more tokens, a common word choice uses fewer tokens

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the earlier Tokens and Tokenization topic, common words typically map to a single token, rare or unusual words often split into several, at genuinely high volume, favoring simpler, more common phrasing where it does not sacrifice clarity can meaningfully reduce token count across millions of calls.
6. Avoiding Token-Wasteful Formatting

blocks.alt: Excessive whitespace or formatting wastes tokens

blocks.text: Unnecessary repeated whitespace, redundant formatting characters, or verbose structural markup can quietly inflate token count without adding any real value, this is exactly the kind of cleanup the earlier Tokens and Tokenization topic worked example demonstrated producing a real, measurable cost reduction.
7. Measuring Total Token Cost Per Request

A practical optimization workflow measures the full token cost per request, input tokens plus output tokens, not just one side of that equation, this connects directly to the metric-driven iteration process covered in the earlier Prompt Iteration topic, applied specifically to token count as the metric being optimized.
8. Token Optimization vs Prompt Compression

These two topics work at different scopes, prompt compression specifically shrinks the input prompt content itself, token optimization is the broader discipline covering input tokens, output tokens, word choice, and formatting together, prompt compression is really one specific technique within this broader token optimization picture.
9. Balancing Token Savings Against Output Quality

blocks.alt: Token savings alone is compared against token savings balanced with output quality

blocks.text: Every token optimization technique carries the same underlying risk covered in the earlier Prompt Compression topic, an overly aggressive max token cap can cut off a response mid-thought, an overly narrow stop sequence can truncate genuinely needed content, every optimization needs to be verified against actual output quality, not applied blindly.
Worked Example

A team running a high volume summarization service notices their average response runs significantly longer than actually needed for their use case, with no explicit length constraint in either the prompt or the API call.

Adding both an explicit instruction requesting a concise summary and a reasonable max token cap on the API call itself reduces average output token count substantially, while testing confirms summary quality and completeness remain acceptable for their actual use case, demonstrating the combined effect of prompt level and API level token control working together.
Common Mistakes

items: Optimizing only input prompt length while ignoring unnecessarily long output responses
Setting a max token cap so aggressive it cuts off responses mid-thought before completing
Not verifying output quality after applying token optimization techniques, assuming savings are automatically safe
Overlooking simple wins like removing wasteful whitespace or overly verbose formatting from a prompt

blocks.text: Practice

Take a prompt and response pair you have generated before, measure the actual input and output token counts, then apply an explicit output length constraint and, if useful, a stop sequence, and compare the total token count and output quality before and after.
Key Takeaway

Token optimization covers the complete picture of token efficiency, both input and output, constraining output length directly, choosing efficient wording, and avoiding wasteful formatting, all measured and verified against actual output quality rather than applied as a blind, unverified cost cutting exercise.
